outputs.L2:
“For all its heroes, ancient Greece held a fatal meaning for Medea: water was death.”  
—Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*

I fixed myself some cereal and discarded the emptied carton. Granddaddy retrieved it from the garbage, shook the remaining dust into a bowl, and flooded those grainy remnants with milk. Staring into his meal, he quietly recalled living through the Depression. He spoke of going into segregated diners and requesting hot water, then stirring ketchup into a cup to create soup. That was my earliest lesson in my own extravagance.

•

Beside my mother in the bathroom, I would wonder aloud why the toilet water had turned red. She answered that she had been eating beets. Perhaps I was not yet old enough for the real explanation: milkflowers shedding crimson petals.

•

At my Catholic school, where we moved together like fish in a shoal, a splendidly packaged box traveled from student to student. Each of us removed part of its wrapping. Only afterward did someone reveal the lesson: the package symbolized a girl’s virginity, a present reserved for her future husband. Who would desire a plaything someone else had already unsealed? Much of the pleasure, we were told, lies in loosening the ribbon yourself. In this way, I learned that ingratitude lived at the center of who I was.

•

Not long ago, I encountered a person in an Irish pub who said the important thing was understanding my own needs. Later, he informed me: what you need is a wife.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s understanding of womanhood, desire, and responsibility is shaped by lessons passed down through both family and religion. From her grandfather’s stories about surviving the Great Depression and racial segregation, she learns that wasting food is not merely careless but shameful. His memories of scarcity and injustice turn every unused resource into evidence of ingratitude. Yet her family also shields her from difficult truths. When she first encounters menstruation, for example, her mother tells her that the blood comes from eating beets, replacing an honest explanation of her body with a comforting fiction.

Catholic school reinforces this atmosphere of secrecy and guilt. There, the speaker is taught to think of female virginity as a precious gift that must be preserved for a future husband. Her body is therefore presented less as her own than as something she must protect for someone else. Taken together, these lessons leave her feeling inherently wasteful, ungrateful, and somehow at fault—whether she is dealing with food, her body, or her desires.

These inherited ideas continue to shape her adult relationships. In a recent encounter, a man confidently claims that he understands what she needs. His certainty culminates in the declaration that what she really needs is a wife. The remark is both revealing and ironic: after a lifetime of being taught to serve, preserve, and sacrifice, the speaker is told that she needs someone who will perform those same forms of care for her.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores how shame is inherited and reinforced through family life, religious education, and intimate relationships. Its fragmented structure mirrors the speaker’s process of remembering: scenes of scarcity, menstruation, virginity, and gendered obligation emerge not as a continuous narrative but as painful lessons that have accumulated over time. Material deprivation becomes inseparable from moral judgment. The speaker learns that wanting more, using too much, or failing to appreciate what she has can be treated as evidence that she is wasteful and ungrateful.

Catholic schooling deepens this sense of guilt by presenting the female body as something that must be controlled, concealed, and preserved. Menstruation is surrounded by embarrassment, while virginity is treated as a measure of purity and value. These teachings deny the speaker a neutral or self-determined relationship with her body. Instead, bodily experience becomes connected to sin, danger, and the expectations of others. Her worth appears to depend on discipline and sacrifice rather than autonomy.

The poem also shows how patriarchal beliefs are transmitted across generations, often through ordinary advice, warnings, and family habits. Women may repeat these lessons because they have learned them as strategies for survival, even when doing so perpetuates harm. As a result, the speaker is taught to minimize her own needs, accept discomfort, and understand femininity as service. In intimate encounters, these expectations continue to shape how she interprets desire, consent, and obligation. She is encouraged to define herself through what others want from her rather than through what she wants for herself.

By placing these memories beside one another, the poem reveals that shame is not a private failing but a social inheritance. Ideas about money, purity, gratitude, and womanhood work together to make the speaker distrust her desires and police her own behavior. The lasting damage of this conditioning lies in its ability to become an inner voice: even when the original authority figures are absent, their judgments remain. Ultimately, the poem exposes how family, religion, and patriarchy teach women to experience their bodies and needs as burdens, while its act of remembering begins to challenge the values that produced that shame.
outputs.L5:
Ancient Greece continues to influence modern literature through its myths and tragedies. One of its most powerful figures is Medea, the sorceress who helps Jason obtain the Golden Fleece, only to be betrayed by him. In Euripides’ tragedy, Medea responds with terrible violence, becoming a complex symbol of love, anger, abandonment, and female power.

American writer Jesmyn Ward reimagines this classical legacy in her novel *Salvage the Bones*. Its young protagonist, Esch, reads about Medea while facing poverty, pregnancy, and the approaching devastation of Hurricane Katrina. Esch recognizes parts of herself in the Greek heroine, particularly Medea’s passionate love and vulnerability. Yet Ward does not simply repeat the ancient story. She places its themes within the experience of a Black family in rural Mississippi, showing how myth can speak across different cultures and historical periods.

Through Medea, Jesmyn Ward creates a bridge between ancient Greece and the modern American South. The comparison gives Esch a language for understanding love, betrayal, survival, and her own emerging identity. At the same time, *Salvage the Bones* transforms the Greek myth: tragedy remains present, but so do family loyalty, resilience, and hope.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem about how family poverty, menstruation, Catholic teachings on virginity, and men’s expectations shape a young woman’s understanding of herself.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory**

At thirteen, I learned the price of everything:

rice by the pound,  
electricity by the hour,  
shame by the silence it purchased.

My mother rinsed plastic bags  
and hung them above the sink  
like small transparent flags  
of a country we could not leave.

The month came red  
and without ceremony.

I folded toilet paper thick as prayer,  
walked carefully through school,  
afraid my body might announce  
what our cupboards already knew:

we could not afford  
for anything to overflow.

On Sundays, the Virgin watched  
from her blue alcove—  
clean, chosen, impossible—  
while Father spoke of purity  
as if a girl were a glass of water  
men would refuse  
once another mouth had touched it.

I tried to make myself clear.

No wanting.  
No anger.  
No stain flowering  
through the back of my skirt.

The boys wanted beauty  
without hunger,  
softness without need.  
Later, men would call me difficult  
for locking the door,  
cold for opening it slowly,  
a tease for having a body  
that did not become theirs  
when noticed.

At home, my father said  
a good girl knows what men are like,  
as though their wanting were weather  
and my life a roof  
responsible for every leak.

So I became useful:

held babies, counted coins,  
kept my knees together,  
my grades high,  
my voice low.

I mistook endurance for virtue.  
I mistook fear for faith.  
I mistook being untouched  
for being whole.

Years passed before I understood  
the Virgin had a body too—  
blood, breath, labor—  
that holiness need not mean  
disappearing.

Now, when the month returns,  
I buy what I need  
without apology.

I leave the box visible  
on the bathroom shelf.

I say no  
as a complete sentence.  
I say yes  
only when it belongs to me.

My body is not the family debt,  
not a parish lesson,  
not a promise made  
to a future husband’s pride.

It is not poor  
because it has needed.

It is not ruined  
because it has bled.

It is mine—  
not immaculate,  
not merchandise,

alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented prose poem that begins with a quotation from Jesmyn Ward’s *Salvage the Bones* and uses cereal, Depression-era survival, “beet” blood, and an unwrapped gift as recurring images.
counterfactuals.output:
“China’s turned on herself.” —Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*

Morning arrives in fragments: cornflakes gone soft in rainwater, the spoon silver as a small surrender. Grandmother says during the Depression they saved everything—bacon grease, buttons, the clean halves of rotten fruit. Hunger taught each object a second life.

On the cutting board, beets open their dark wrists. Beet blood stains the towel, the floor, our fingerprints. No one is hurt, we keep saying. No one is hurt.

The gift waits beneath the table, unwrapped. A box with no ribbon, no name. We circle it with our bowls of cereal, listening to the flakes collapse.

Grandmother saved sugar in a blue jar. Saved string in a drawer. Saved stories until they soured. In 1933, she says, an onion was an inheritance. A heel of bread was a feast you chewed slowly enough to make into weather.

Again the beets. Again their harmless blood. We scrub, but the sink remembers.

By noon, the cereal is paste. By evening, the unwrapped gift has become another mouth. We do not open it. We know survival sometimes means refusing to learn what has been given.

Outside, the garden keeps its red secrets underground.

Inside, we lift our spoons. We eat what is left.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lowercase confessional poem in four sections separated by bullets, exploring the speaker’s learned feelings of wastefulness, shame, and ingratitude before ending with a man saying, “what you need is a wife.”
counterfactuals.output:
i.

i learned wastefulness at the table,  
where the bruised fruit watched me  
choose hunger over gratitude.  
my mother saved every jar, every ribbon,  
while i let whole afternoons spoil  
in the blue light of my room.

•

ii.

shame came dressed as cleanliness:  
a rinsed plate, a folded apology,  
my hands hiding behind my back.  
i mistook needing for greed  
and silence for being good,  
then wondered why my mouth ached.

•

iii.

i have been ungrateful for warmth,  
for rent paid late but paid,  
for the people who carried me  
without asking what i weighed.  
even now, kindness enters  
and i inventory the exits.

•

iv.

i confess this to a man  
who nods as if my life  
were a sink of unwashed cups,  
as if loneliness were a chore  
another body should inherit.  
he leans back and says,  
“what you need is a wife.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
